summary: Hunter Mountain's 1917 Aermotor LS-40 tower, the state's oldest active fire-watch site (begun 1909), was nearly removed in the 1990s but was restored and is now a volunteer-run weekend museum.

facts.design: Aermotor LS-40, 60-foot steel tower; preceded by a 1909 wooden tower built from timbers found on the summit
facts.status_note: Restored; no longer used for active fire detection, operated as a staffed-by-volunteers historic site/museum

staffing.status: volunteer, weekends only (Memorial Day through Columbus Day)

access.note: Reached via marked NYSDEC hiking trails shared with equestrian use; cab staffed by volunteers on some weekends.

visit.trail_note: Marked DEC-blazed trail to the summit; water and shelter available about a mile below the summit.

events.note: First fire-observation station established on Hunter Mountain, a wooden tower built from timbers found on the mountaintop, about 40 feet below the true summit, at 4,000 feet elevation.
Present 60-foot steel Aermotor LS-40 tower erected next to the original wood tower site.
Tower dismantled and re-erected at its current location on the true summit (4,040 feet).
Added to the National Register of Historic Places after DEC had recommended the deteriorated tower for removal in the 1990s.
Tower turned 100 years old; centennial marked with a plaque dedicated to past observers, attended by the last known surviving observer.

evidence.supports: 1909 wooden tower, 1917 steel tower, 1950 relocation to summit
evidence.quote: Established in 1909 with a tower made of timbers found at the mountain top the station was established at the 4,000 foot elevation of the mountain, 40 feet shy of the true summit. In 1917 the present 60' steel Aermotor LS-40 tower was erected next to the wood tower site, and it remained at the 4,000 foot elevation until in 1950 the tower was dismantled and re-erected at the current location on the summit of 4,040 feet.

evidence.supports: Centennial celebration in 2017 with plaque and surviving observer
evidence.quote: Hunter Mountain Fire Tower turned one hundred years old in 2017. The NYSDEC in cooperation with the Hunter Mountain Fire Tower Committee celebrated this event with the unveiling of a plaque dedicated to the Observers who served on the fire tower. The event included the last known surviving Observer being in attendance.

evidence.supports: Volunteer weekend staffing via Catskill Fire Tower Project since 1996
evidence.quote: Since 1996, the Hunter Mountain Fire Tower has been part of the Catskill Fire Tower Project, a joint venture of the NYSDEC, the CCCD, and the 5 Fire Tower Committees... the tower has been staffed by volunteers of the Committee each weekend from Memorial through Columbus Day.

evidence.supports: Trail access, shared equestrian path, water/shelter a mile below summit
evidence.quote: Access is by clearly marked and well defined NYSDEC blazed trails, Hike is over a shared foot and Equine path, from a slightly hidden parking area. Water and shelter are available about a mile down the trail from the summit, and lookout.

evidence.supports: First of 23 state towers, DEC recommended removal in 1990s, NRHP listing in 1997, restoration
evidence.quote: It was the first of 23 fire lookout towers built by the state in the region, and the next-to-last of the five still standing to be abandoned... After it fell into disrepair in the 1990s and was recommended for removal by the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC)... it was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1997. Local enthusiasts were able to raise money, matched by DEC, to restore the tower and adjacent observer's cabin

evidence.supports: Highest fire tower still standing in New York
evidence.quote: It is the highest fire tower still standing in the state and the second-highest in the entire Northeast.

evidence.supports: Program launched after 1903/1908 drought fires, modeled on Maine's observation towers
evidence.quote: Severe fires during droughts in 1903 and 1908 caused thousands of dollars in damages and led to public calls for better fire control efforts... His counterpart in Maine, E.E. Ring, wrote back to one of his inquiries highly recommending the use of strategically placed observation towers similar to the nine his state had already installed.

notes_for_editor: Brief's access field was 'unknown'; sources support public/volunteer-staffed access, consider updating. Height given in brief record omitted; 60 feet converted to 18.3m here from NHLR description, not from the brief's own height_m field (brief had none).
